query: For automotive exhaust catalysts, what single intervention could improve catalytic activity and durability while reducing platinum-group-metal consumption? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should hold, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Automotive exhaust catalysts synthesized via NaCl‐templated single-atom catalyst (SAC) methods, which achieve atomically dispersed platinum-group metals, will exhibit enhanced catalytic activity and durability while reducing precious metal consumption compared to conventional nanoparticle-based catalysts.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional automotive exhaust catalysts that deploy supported platinum-group metal nanoparticles on oxide supports (e.g., Pd/γ-Al2O3).
generation.intervention: Implement NaCl-templated synthesis to produce SACs with atomically dispersed platinum-group metals through templated 3D honeycomb architectures featuring in-plane M–Nx coordination.
generation.conditions: Operation under typical automotive exhaust conditions—high temperatures and cyclic oxidizing environments—and using synthesis protocols that reliably induce atomically dispersed active sites.
generation.structural_mediator: The NaCl templating process facilitates a 3D honeycomb-like morphology that enforces atomic dispersion of the platinum-group metals into well-defined coordination environments.
generation.mechanism: Atomic dispersion maximizes the exposure of active sites and enhances electronic interactions with the support, which improves reaction kinetics at lower metal loadings. Additionally, the unique microstructure decreases tendencies for sintering during thermal cycling, thereby enhancing durability.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventional nanoparticle catalysts, the SAC catalysts are expected to achieve higher catalytic conversion rates of exhaust gases and sustain their activity over extended thermal cycling while requiring less platinum-group metal loading.
generation.baseline: Catalytic performance and durability of conventional nanoparticle-based automotive exhaust catalysts (e.g., Pd/γ-Al2O3).
generation.boundary: This improvement is anticipated under standard automotive exhaust operating temperatures and oxidative/reductive cycles; results may differ if the NaCl templating process does not uniformly yield true atomic dispersion.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of improvement in activity and durability is uncertain due to potential synthesis variability and operational complexities in real exhaust conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two groups of catalysts: one batch using the conventional nanoparticle-based method and a second batch using the NaCl-templated SAC synthesis. Both catalyst groups will be coated on identical supports and subjected to simulated automotive exhaust conditions (including high-temperature cycling and redox fluctuations).
measurements: Catalytic conversion efficiency (e.g., NOx conversion rates) under steady-state and cyclic conditions.
Durability tests measuring activity retention after prolonged thermal cycling.
Quantification of platinum-group metal loadings in relation to catalytic performance.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the NaCl-templated SAC catalysts do not demonstrate statistically significant improvements in catalytic activity and durability, or if the platinum-group metal consumption is not measurably reduced compared to conventional catalysts under identical testing conditions, the hypothesis will be falsified.

It is known that the PdO/Al2O3 catalyst is not stable at high temperatures due to PdO reduction and surface area loss, which necessitates the exploration of mixed oxide catalysts [,]. La2O3 is commonly added to enhance PdO stability and preserve γ-Al2O3’s surface area, improving the catalyst’s durability []. Complex catalysts are synthesized by the co-impregnation of Pd and La salts, often with a third element, to obtain a three-element system on γ-Al2O3 or ceramic supports. AbstractSingle-atom catalysts (SACs) with featured active sites exhibit exceptional catalytic activity and selectivity in catalysis. However, their scalable synthesis and precise control of structure coordination for on-demand atomic configurations remain the bottlenecks in practical applications. In this work, a facile and scalable strategy is developed to achieve massive production of varying molecular-coordinated single- and multi metal-based SACs. Low-cost NaCl is used as a recyclable and green template. Its nature of temperature-induced confinement with a phase change of ion dissociation can direct 3D honeycomb-like morphology of SACs with different coordinations of in-plane M–Nx (x = 4 or 6) at lower temperature and axial M–Cl at above melting point of NaCl (900 °C), as demonstrated by controlled experiments and theoretical computations. A library of 25 distinct SACs and high-entropy SACs containing five metals with tailored structure are synthesized in a mass yield ranging from 18.3% to 50.9%.
